claim: Aggregation and accumulation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau proteins are a defining feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology.
source: Aggregation and accumulation of amyloid-beta (Aβ) and tau proteins are a defining feature of Alzheimer's disease (AD) pathophysiology (Braak and Braak, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citation to Braak and Braak, 1991

claim: Disruption of the fine balance between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal activity has emerged as a potential driver for network dysfunction contributing to cognitive deficits in AD.
source: Although the mechanisms by which AD proteinopathy exerts its effects remain an area of active research, disruption of the fine balance between excitatory and inhibitory neuronal activity has emerged as a potential driver for network dysfunction contributing to cognitive deficits in AD (Palop et al., 2006; Harris et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Palop et al., 2006 and Harris et al., 2020

claim: Preclinical AD models have demonstrated direct effects of tau and Aβ leading to impaired function in excitatory pyramidal neurons as well as inhibitory interneurons.
source: Preclinical AD models have demonstrated direct effects of tau and Aβ leading to impaired function in excitatory pyramidal neurons as well as inhibitory interneurons (Palop et al., 2007; Hoover et al., 2010; Sun et al., 2012; Verret et al., 2012; Palop and Mucke, 2016; Zhou et al., 2017; Busche et al., 2019; Zott et al., 2019; Harris et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2021 ).
evidence: Supported by multiple citations to preclinical studies

claim: In patients with AD, abnormalities in brain oscillations are a display of perturbed balance of excitation and inhibition in local circuits.
source: In patients with AD, abnormalities in brain oscillations (Ranasinghe et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2018; Maestú et al., 2019; Babiloni et al., 2020; Ranasinghe et al., 2020), which are essentially determined by relative contributions of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents (Buzsáki et al., 2012), are a display of perturbed balance of excitation and inhibition in local circuits.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies and knowledge about oscillations

claim: Clinical studies have demonstrated associations between abnormal oscillatory signatures and AD proteinopathy.
source: However, despite the fact that clinical studies have demonstrated associations between abnormal oscillatory signatures and AD proteinopathy (Nakamura et al., 2018; Smailovic et al., 2018; Pusil et al., 2019; Ranasinghe et al., 2020; Ranasinghe et al., 2021), the electrophysiological basis of aberrant excitatory and inhibitory activity of neuronal cell populations and how these relate to Aβ and tau remain largely unknown in patients with AD.
evidence: Supported by citations to clinical studies

claim: Twenty patients with AD and 35 age-matched controls were included in this study.
source: Twenty patients with AD (diagnostic criteria for probable AD or mild cognitive impairment due to AD) (Albert et al., 2011; McKhann et al., 2011; Jack et al., 2018) and 35 age-matched controls were included in this study (Table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of study sample size

claim: All AD patients underwent PET with tau-specific radiotracer, 18F-flortaucipir and Aβ-specific radiotracer, 11C-PIB.
source: All AD patients underwent PET with tau-specific radiotracer, 18F-flortaucipir and Aβ-specific radiotracer, 11C-PIB.
evidence: Direct statement of imaging methods used

claim: Patients with AD showed a clear leftward shift in their power spectra when compared to age-matched controls.
source: Patients with AD showed a clear leftward shift in their power spectra when compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: Direct statement of observed spectral changes

claim: AD patients showed a reduced spectral power within alpha (CI, 58.04–59.85 dB, 60.33–61.69 dB, AD and controls, respectively) and beta (CI, 53.16–54.11B, 56.03–56.75 dB, AD and controls, respectively) but increased power within delta–theta bands (60.14–61.79 dB, 57.60–58.85 dB, AD and controls, respectively).
source: Specifically, AD patients showed a reduced spectral power within alpha (CI, 58.04–59.85 dB, 60.33–61.69 dB, AD and controls, respectively) and beta (CI, 53.16–54.11B, 56.03–56.75 dB, AD and controls, respectively) but increased power within delta–theta bands (60.14–61.79 dB, 57.60–58.85 dB, AD and controls, respectively) (Figure 1A, B).
evidence: Quantitative data with confidence intervals and reference to Figure 1A, B

claim: A direct region-wise comparison showed a frontal predominant spatial distribution for the spectral power increase within delta–theta and a posterior predominant distribution for the spectral power reduction in alpha and beta, in patients with AD.
source: A direct region-wise comparison showed a frontal predominant spatial distribution for the spectral power increase within delta–theta and a posterior predominant distribution for the spectral power reduction in alpha and beta, in patients with AD (Figure 1C; Appendix 1—figure 1).
evidence: Direct statement of regional patterns with reference to Figure 1C

claim: AD patients have significantly increased time-constant parameters of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (τe and τi) than controls.
source: Statistical mixed models with repeated measures demonstrated that AD patients have significantly increased time-constant parameters of excitatory and inhibitory neurons (τe and τi) than controls (Figure 1E; τe: CI, 15.27–16.19, 11.49–12.18; p < 0.0001; τi: CI, 16.03–16.96, 15.02–15.73; p = 0.0002, AD and controls, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis results with confidence intervals and p-values, reference to Figure 1E

claim: AD patients showed increased gee and reduced gii compared to controls indicating abnormal neural gains in both excitatory and inhibitory subpopulations.
source: Furthermore, AD patients showed increased gee and reduced gii compared to controls indicating abnormal neural gains in both excitatory and inhibitory subpopulations (Figure 1E; gee: CI, 1.88–2.21, 1.59–1.87; p = 0.0005; gii: CI, 3.04–3.42, 3.52–3.81; p = 0.0003, AD and controls, respectively).
evidence: Statistical analysis results with confidence intervals and p-values, reference to Figure 1E

claim: Increased excitatory time-constant (τe) was positively correlated with tau-tracer uptake.
source: linear mixed-effects models showed that increased τe was correlated with higher tau-tracer uptake, while increased τi was correlated with higher Aβ-tracer uptake (Figure 3A, D; τe: tau, t = 4.11, p < 0.0001; τi: Aβ, t = 3.38, p = 0.0008).
evidence: Statistical analysis results with t-values and p-values, reference to Figure 3A, D

claim: Increased inhibitory time-constant (τi) was positively correlated with Aβ-tracer uptake.
source: linear mixed-effects models showed that increased τe was correlated with higher tau-tracer uptake, while increased τi was correlated with higher Aβ-tracer uptake (Figure 3A, D; τe: tau, t = 4.11, p < 0.0001; τi: Aβ, t = 3.38, p = 0.0008).
evidence: Statistical analysis results with t-values and p-values, reference to Figure 3A, D

claim: There were no correlations between τe and Aβ-tracer uptake and between τi and tau-tracer uptake.
source: In contrast, there were no correlations between τe and Aβ-tracer uptake and between τi and tau-tracer uptake (Figure 3B, C; τe: Aβ, t = −1.59, p = 0.1131; τi: tau, t = 0.54, p = 0.5863).
evidence: Statistical analysis results showing non-significant correlations, reference to Figure 3B, C

claim: Altered neural gains did not show statistically significant associations to either flortaucipir or 11C-PiB uptakes.
source: In contrast to time-constant associations, altered neural gains did not show statistically significant associations to either flortaucipir or 11C-PiB uptakes (Appendix 1—figure 3).
evidence: Direct statement of non-significant associations with reference to Appendix figure

claim: Delta–theta power was only associated with Aβ (positive correlation) and showed no associations to tau.
source: For example, delta–theta was only associated with Aβ (positive correlation) and showed no associations to tau (Figure 4A, B).
evidence: Direct statement of associations with reference to Figure 4A, B

claim: Alpha and beta power spectra showed significant associations to both tau and Aβ, where higher tau reduced spectral power and higher Aβ increased spectral power.
source: In contrast, alpha and beta power spectra showed significant associations to both tau and Aβ, where higher tau reduced spectral power and higher Aβ increased spectral power (Figure 4D, E, G, H).
evidence: Direct statement of associations with reference to Figure 4D, E, G, H

claim: Including regional cortical atrophy as a covariate into the models did not influence the relationships between spectral changes and tau/Aβ, indicating that spectral changes are robust to neuronal loss.
source: Including regional cortical atrophy as a covariate into the models did not influence these relationships, indicating that spectral changes are robust to neuronal loss (Appendix 1—figure 4).
evidence: Direct statement of covariate analysis results with reference to Appendix figure

claim: Aβ modulation of delta–theta power was significantly mediated through τi in addition to direct modulation.
source: We found that Aβ modulation of delta–theta power was significantly mediated through τi in addition to direct modulation (Figure 4C).
evidence: Direct statement of mediation analysis results with reference to Figure 4C

claim: Tau modulation of alpha power was significantly mediated through τe in addition to the direct modulation.
source: We also found that tau modulation of alpha power was significantly mediated through τe in addition to the direct modulation (Figure 4F), whereas Aβ modulation of alpha power was only through a direct effect.
evidence: Direct statement of mediation analysis results with reference to Figure 4F

claim: Aβ modulation of alpha power was only through a direct effect.
source: We also found that tau modulation of alpha power was significantly mediated through τe in addition to the direct modulation (Figure 4F), whereas Aβ modulation of alpha power was only through a direct effect.
evidence: Direct statement of mediation analysis results

claim: Tau as well as Aβ modulation of beta power occurred only though direct effects.
source: Tau as well as Aβ modulation of beta power occurred only though direct effects (Figure 4I).
evidence: Direct statement of mediation analysis results with reference to Figure 4I

claim: This is the first study, in patients with AD, showing quantitative links between altered neuronal subpopulation dynamics of excitatory and inhibitory function, and abnormal accumulations of tau and Aβ.
source: This is the first study, in patients with AD, showing quantitative links between altered neuronal subpopulation dynamics of excitatory and inhibitory function, and abnormal accumulations of tau and Aβ.
evidence: Direct statement of novelty claim

claim: Neuropathological studies in human patients with AD detailing the morphology and location of cells that accumulate tau and degenerate indicate an increased vulnerability of excitatory neurons to tau-related pathomechanisms.
source: For example, neuropathological studies in human patients with AD detailing the morphology and location of cells that accumulate tau and degenerate indicate an increased vulnerability of excitatory neurons to tau-related pathomechanisms (Hyman et al., 1984; Braak and Braak, 1991).
evidence: Supported by citations to Hyman et al., 1984 and Braak and Braak, 1991

claim: Mice expressing mutant human tau demonstrate impaired synaptic transmission of glutamate leading to reduced firing of pyramidal neurons.
source: In basic science studies, mice expressing mutant human tau demonstrate impaired synaptic transmission of glutamate leading to reduced firing of pyramidal neurons (Hoover et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2019) while tau reduction in transgenic mice produce an overall decrease in baseline excitatory neuronal activity and modulate the inhibitory neuronal activity leading to reduced network excitation (Chang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to preclinical studies

claim: Tau reduction in transgenic mice produce an overall decrease in baseline excitatory neuronal activity and modulate the inhibitory neuronal activity leading to reduced network excitation.
source: In basic science studies, mice expressing mutant human tau demonstrate impaired synaptic transmission of glutamate leading to reduced firing of pyramidal neurons (Hoover et al., 2010; Fu et al., 2017; Fu et al., 2019) while tau reduction in transgenic mice produce an overall decrease in baseline excitatory neuronal activity and modulate the inhibitory neuronal activity leading to reduced network excitation (Chang et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citation to Chang et al., 2021

claim: The collective insight from preclinical observations indicates a relative vulnerability of excitatory function in neural networks to tau and a resulting network hypoactivity.
source: The collective insight from these observations indicates a relative vulnerability of excitatory function in neural networks to tau and a resulting network hypoactivity (Harris et al., 2020).
evidence: Inference from preclinical studies, supported by citation to Harris et al., 2020

claim: Accumulation of Aβ is extracellular.
source: In contrast to intracellular aggregates of tau, accumulation of Aβ is extracellular (Braak and Braak, 1991; Nagy et al., 1995).
evidence: Supported by citations to Braak and Braak, 1991 and Nagy et al., 1995

claim: AD basic science models have demonstrated a range of Aβ-associated pathomechanisms that ranges from toxic effects of different Aβ forms affecting both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic functions.
source: AD basic science models have demonstrated a range of Aβ-associated pathomechanisms that ranges from toxic effects of different Aβ forms affecting both excitatory and inhibitory synaptic functions (Meyer-Luehmann et al., 2008; Busche et al., 2012; Busche et al., 2015; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to preclinical studies

claim: A potential means by which Aβ leads to network dysfunction in animal models of AD is abnormal hyperactivity in cortical and hippocampal neurons.
source: A potential means by which Aβ leads to network dysfunction in animal models of AD is abnormal hyperactivity in cortical and hippocampal neurons (Palop and Mucke, 2016).
evidence: Supported by citation to Palop and Mucke, 2016

claim: Compelling evidence from AD transgenic mice indicate impaired inhibitory synaptic function as a contributory cause for Aβ-related neuronal hyperactivity.
source: Compelling evidence from AD transgenic mice indicate impaired inhibitory synaptic function as a contributory cause for Aβ-related neuronal hyperactivity (Busche et al., 2008; Busche et al., 2012; Verret et al., 2012).
evidence: Supported by citations to preclinical studies

claim: Basic science experiments have identified reduced inhibitory interneuron activity as well as aberrant glutamate transmission as potential underlying causes of network hyperactivity in AD transgenic mice.
source: Basic science experiments indeed have identified reduced inhibitory interneuron activity as well as aberrant glutamate transmission as potential underlying causes of network hyperactivity in AD transgenic mice (Busche et al., 2008; Verret et al., 2012; Zott et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citations to preclinical studies

claim: A key finding from preclinical AD models is that cellular-level changes associated with tau and Aβ produces a combined functional consequence of altered excitatory–inhibitory balance in neural networks.
source: A key finding from preclinical AD models is that cellular-level changes associated with tau and Aβ produces a combined functional consequence of altered excitatory–inhibitory balance in neural networks (Palop and Mucke, 2016; Harris et al., 2020; Chang et al., 2021; Maestú et al., 2021).
evidence: Supported by citations to preclinical studies

claim: The emerging picture from basic science models of AD suggest that abnormally increased neuronal activity associated with Aβ most likely dominate during preclinical stage of the disease.
source: The emerging picture from basic science models of AD also suggest that abnormally increased neuronal activity associated with Aβ most likely dominate during preclinical stage of the disease (Zott et al., 2019), whereas the firing suppression of tau will become predominant at later stages (Busche et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Zott et al., 2019

claim: The firing suppression of tau will become predominant at later stages of AD.
source: The emerging picture from basic science models of AD also suggest that abnormally increased neuronal activity associated with Aβ most likely dominate during preclinical stage of the disease (Zott et al., 2019), whereas the firing suppression of tau will become predominant at later stages (Busche et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Busche et al., 2019

claim: Abnormal neural gains may represent an early effect of soluble neurotoxins, while abnormal time-constants may represent dynamic effects of network changes indicating progressive pathophysiological events.
source: As such it is possible that abnormal neural gains may represent an early effect of soluble neurotoxins, while abnormal time-constants may represent dynamic effects of network changes indicatingprogressive pathophysiological events.
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the data and known biology

claim: Oscillations regulate the top-down processing of local neuronal firing and facilitate long-range interactions.
source: Although a unifying principle governing the physiology of rhythmic oscillations remains obscure, a commonly accepted principle is that oscillations regulate the top-down processing of local neuronal firing and facilitate long-range interactions (Uhlhaas et al., 2009).
evidence: Supported by citation to Uhlhaas et al., 2009

claim: Delta–theta oscillations are positive top-down modulators of local neural activity whereas the power of alpha and beta exert an inhibitory modulation of irrelevant neuronal activity thus reducing the neural noise.
source: The prominent view in the current literature is that delta–theta oscillations are positive top-down modulators of local neural activity whereas the power of alpha and beta exert an inhibitory modulation of irrelevant neuronal activity thus reducing the neural noise (Klimesch, 1999).
evidence: Supported by citation to Klimesch, 1999

claim: Higher delta–theta power associated with increased Aβ may predispose a dysregulated increase of local firing.
source: We posit that higher delta–theta power associated with increased Aβ therefore may predispose a dysregulated increase of local firing (Figure 5, left panel).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the study findings and reference to Figure 5

claim: In patients with epilepsy increased focal and generalized slow waves are characteristic features during the interictal period.
source: In patients with epilepsy increased focal and generalized slow waves are characteristic features during the interictal period, although the mechanistic relationship between network hyperexcitability and slow oscillations remains unknown.
evidence: Statement of known clinical observation in epilepsy

claim: In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy higher incidence of slow waves are associated with greater volume loss in medial temporal lobe structures.
source: In patients with temporal lobe epilepsy higher incidence of slow waves are associated with greater volume loss in medial temporal lobe structures (Cascino et al., 1996; Cendes et al., 1996).
evidence: Supported by citations to Cascino et al., 1996 and Cendes et al., 1996

claim: The relationship between Aβ and atrophy in AD is weak as the two phenomena are widely apart in temporal evolution and anatomical distribution.
source: Although it is possible that Aβ-associated unknown mechanisms may relate to both neuronal death and hyperexcitability, the relationship between Aβ and atrophy in AD is weak as the two phenomena are widely apart in temporal evolution and anatomical distribution.
evidence: Statement based on established knowledge about AD pathophysiology

claim: Alpha oscillations are considered as inhibitory gain controllers of local circuits.
source: Because alpha oscillations are considered as inhibitory gain controllers of local circuits (Klimesch et al., 2007; Lorincz et al., 2009), we posit that a net reduction of alpha may yet again be favorable for a status of dysregulated network activity (Figure 5, right panel).
evidence: Supported by citations to Klimesch et al., 2007 and Lorincz et al., 2009

claim: A net reduction of alpha may be favorable for a status of dysregulated network activity.
source: Because alpha oscillations are considered as inhibitory gain controllers of local circuits (Klimesch et al., 2007; Lorincz et al., 2009), we posit that a net reduction of alpha may yet again be favorable for a status of dysregulated network activity (Figure 5, right panel).
evidence: Speculative reasoning based on the study findings and reference to Figure 5

claim: Individuals with preclinical stages of AD and APOE4 carriers who carry an elevated risk of developing AD show increased alpha power and synchrony in select regions including medial frontal and posterior parietal cortices.
source: Individuals with preclinical stages of AD and APOE4 carriers who carry an elevated risk of developing AD show increased alpha power and synchrony in select regions including medial frontal and posterior parietal cortices (Cuesta et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2018; Pusil et al., 2019), whereas in patients with AD dementia syndrome the alpha power and long-range synchrony are reduced (Sami et al., 2018; Ranasinghe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to previous studies

claim: In patients with AD dementia syndrome the alpha power and long-range synchrony are reduced.
source: Individuals with preclinical stages of AD and APOE4 carriers who carry an elevated risk of developing AD show increased alpha power and synchrony in select regions including medial frontal and posterior parietal cortices (Cuesta et al., 2015; Nakamura et al., 2018; Pusil et al., 2019), whereas in patients with AD dementia syndrome the alpha power and long-range synchrony are reduced (Sami et al., 2018; Ranasinghe et al., 2020).
evidence: Supported by citations to Sami et al., 2018 and Ranasinghe et al., 2020

claim: Aβ-positive cognitively normal participants have higher alpha power than Aβ-negative cognitively normal.
source: For example, a study using Aβ-PET in cognitively normal controls and MCI patients showed that Aβ-positive cognitively normal participants have higher alpha power than Aβ-negative cognitively normal whereas, Aβ-positive MCI patients had reduced alpha spectral power compared to cognitively normal regardless of Aβ status (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018

claim: Aβ-positive MCI patients had reduced alpha spectral power compared to cognitively normal regardless of Aβ status.
source: For example, a study using Aβ-PET in cognitively normal controls and MCI patients showed that Aβ-positive cognitively normal participants have higher alpha power than Aβ-negative cognitively normal whereas, Aβ-positive MCI patients had reduced alpha spectral power compared to cognitively normal regardless of Aβ status (Nakamura et al., 2018).
evidence: Supported by citation to Nakamura et al., 2018

claim: Hyperactive effects of Aβ dominate in the preclinical and prodromal stages of AD with subsequent effects of tau and the complex synergy of both proteins leading to hypoactivity in neural circuits.
source: These data support the hypothesis that hyperactive effects of Aβ dominate in the preclinical and prodromal stages of AD with subsequent effects of tau and the complex synergy of both proteins leading to hypoactivity in neural circuits.
evidence: Inference from cited studies and current findings

claim: A recent study using a nonlinear NMM showed consistent findings of a positive relationship between inhibitory time-constant and higher Aβ suggesting an association between Aβ accumulation and spectral slowing.
source: Furthermore, using a nonlinear NMM a recent study also showed consistent findings of a positive relationship between inhibitory time-constant and higher Aβ suggesting an association between Aβ accumulation and spectral slowing (Stefanovski et al., 2019).
evidence: Supported by citation to Stefanovski et al., 2019

claim: Recent comparisons among different models demonstrate that linear models sufficiently capture neuroimaging data with higher accuracy compared to nonlinear models.
source: While linearizing is a simplification of the detailed underlying biophysics, recent comparisons among different models demonstrate that linear models sufficiently capture neuroimaging data with higher accuracy compared to nonlinear models.
evidence: Statement based on model comparison literature

claim: PET signal represents the deposited proteins and is mostly insensitive to soluble forms of proteins.
source: Second, PET signal represents the deposited proteins and is mostly insensitive to soluble forms of proteins, although basic science models suggest that soluble oligomers are concentrated around deposited proteins (Busche et al., 2008).
evidence: Statement of PET imaging limitation with citation

claim: Basic science models suggest that soluble oligomers are concentrated around deposited proteins.
source: Second, PET signal represents the deposited proteins and is mostly insensitive to soluble forms of proteins, although basic science models suggest that soluble oligomers are concentrated around deposited proteins (Busche et al., 2008).
evidence: Supported by citation to Busche et al., 2008

claim: Flortaucipir has known off-target binding in the basal ganglia, choroid plexus, and the meninges.
source: Another limitation includes the known off-target binding of flortaucipir in the basal ganglia, choroid plexus, and the meninges.
evidence: Statement of known limitation of flortaucipir tracer

claim: Off-target sources of flortaucipir signal are unlikely to have driven the study results because the flortaucipir increases were seen in brain areas remote from these sites.
source: However, these off-target sources of signal are unlikely to have driven our results because the flortaucipir increases in the current study were seen in brain areas remote from these sites.
evidence: Inference based on spatial distribution of findings

claim: Patients with AD showed abnormal excitatory and inhibitory time-constants and neural gains compared to age-matched controls.
source: Patients with AD showed abnormal excitatory and inhibitory time-constants and neural gains compared to age-matched controls.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing results

claim: Increased excitatory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher tau depositions.
source: Increased excitatory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher tau depositions while increased inhibitory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher Aβ depositions.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing results

claim: Increased inhibitory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher Aβ depositions.
source: Increased excitatory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher tau depositions while increased inhibitory time-constants distinctly correlated with higher Aβ depositions.
evidence: Direct statement from abstract summarizing results

claim: The regional patterns of increased excitatory time-constants and neural gains showed the highest changes in a spatial pattern involving the temporal lobe and the precuneus.
source: The regional patterns of increased excitatory time-constants and neural gains showed the highest changes in a spatial pattern involving thetemporal lobe and the precuneus (Figure 2A, C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2A, C

claim: Increased inhibitory time-constants showed a distributed spatial pattern involving frontal and parietal cortices.
source: Increased inhibitory time-constants showed a distributed spatial pattern involving frontal and parietal cortices (Figure 2B), while the reduced inhibitory neural gains showed the highest reductions in the right temporal and posterior parietal regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2B

claim: The reduced inhibitory neural gains showed the highest reductions in the right temporal and posterior parietal regions.
source: Increased inhibitory time-constants showed a distributed spatial pattern involving frontal and parietal cortices (Figure 2B), while the reduced inhibitory neural gains showed the highest reductions in the right temporal and posterior parietal regions (Figure 2C).
evidence: Direct statement with reference to Figure 2C

claim: Twelve AD patients in this study cohort overlapped with a previous multimodal imaging investigation of long-range synchrony assay.
source: Twelve AD patients in this study cohort overlapped with our previous multimodal imaging investigation of long-range synchrony assay (Ranasinghe et al., 2020).
evidence: Direct statement about study cohort overlap

claim: The mean MMSE score of AD patients was 22.8 ± 4.5.
source: On average, the patients were mild to moderately impaired with a mean MMSE score of 22.8 ± 4.5 (MMSE range: 22–26), mean CDR of 0.72 ± 0.47 (CDR range: 0.5–0.8), and mean CDR-SOB of 3.8 ± 2.5, with characteristic cognitive deficits (Table 1; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of clinical data

claim: The mean CDR of AD patients was 0.72 ± 0.47.
source: On average, the patients were mild to moderately impaired with a mean MMSE score of 22.8 ± 4.5 (MMSE range: 22–26), mean CDR of 0.72 ± 0.47 (CDR range: 0.5–0.8), and mean CDR-SOB of 3.8 ± 2.5, with characteristic cognitive deficits (Table 1; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of clinical data

claim: The mean CDR-SOB of AD patients was 3.8 ± 2.5.
source: On average, the patients were mild to moderately impaired with a mean MMSE score of 22.8 ± 4.5 (MMSE range: 22–26), mean CDR of 0.72 ± 0.47 (CDR range: 0.5–0.8), and mean CDR-SOB of 3.8 ± 2.5, with characteristic cognitive deficits (Table 1; Appendix 1—table 1).
evidence: Direct statement of clinical data

claim: Distinctive association of tau with excitatory time-constants and Aβ with inhibitory time-constants may support the hypothesis of distinct roles of tau- and Aβ-mediated pathomechanisms on excitatory and inhibitory synaptic functions.
source: Distinctive association of tau with excitatory time-constants and Aβ with inhibitory time-constants may support the hypothesis of distinct roles of tau- and Aβ-mediated pathomechanisms on excitatory and inhibitory synaptic functions.
evidence: Inference from the study findings

claim: Frequency-specific oscillatory signatures provide attractive biomarkers to track the dynamics of AD pathophysiology in the next generation of AD therapeutic trials.
source: Frequency-specific oscillatory signatures provide attractive biomarkers to track the dynamics of AD pathophysiology in the next generation of AD therapeutic trials.
evidence: Inference and speculation based on study findings

claim: The excitatory and inhibitory time-constant parameters characterize the duration of the neural responses in each neuronal subpopulation.
source: The excitatory and inhibitory time-constant parameters characterize the duration of the neural responses (modeled by a Gamma-shaped function) in each neuronal subpopulation, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement explaining model parameters

claim: Time-constant parameters characterize the rate at which a local signal dissipates in absence of other inputs.
source: It also characterizes the rate at which a local signal dissipates in absence of other inputs.
evidence: Direct statement explaining model parameters

claim: A lower time-constant indicates a faster rate of change in signals while a higher time-constant indicates a slower rate.
source: A lower time-constant indicates a faster rate of change in signals while a higher time-constant indicates a slower rate.
evidence: Direct statement explaining model parameters

claim: The excitatory and inhibitory gain parameters correspond to the postsynaptic gain on the impulse response function of each neuronal subpopulation.
source: The excitatory and inhibitory gain parameters correspond to the postsynaptic gain on the impulse response function of each neuronal subpopulation, respectively.
evidence: Direct statement explaining model parameters

claim: The goodness of fit of the model was estimated by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient between the simulated model power spectra and the empirical source localized MEG spectra for frequencies 1–35 Hz.
source: The goodness of fit of the model was estimated by calculating the Pearson's correlation coefficient between the simulated model power spectra and the empirical source localized MEG spectra for frequencies 1–35 Hz.
evidence: Direct statement of modeling methodology

claim: Oscillations are essentially determined by relative contributions of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents.
source: In patients with AD, abnormalities in brain oscillations (Ranasinghe et al., 2014; Nakamura et al., 2018; Maestú et al., 2019; Babiloni et al., 2020; Ranasinghe et al., 2020), which are essentially determined by relative contributions of excitatory and inhibitory synaptic currents (Buzsáki et al., 2012), are a display of perturbed balance of excitation and inhibition in local circuits.
evidence: Supported by citation to Buzsáki et al., 2012

claim: Low-frequency delta–theta and mid-frequency alpha and beta oscillations employ diverse physiological mechanisms determined by different ionic currents.
source: Low-frequency delta–theta and mid-frequency alpha and beta oscillations employ diverse physiological mechanisms determined by different ionic currents (Wang, 2010) and have distinct functional roles (Engel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citations to Wang, 2010 and Engel et al., 2001

claim: Low-frequency delta–theta and mid-frequency alpha and beta oscillations have distinct functional roles.
source: Low-frequency delta–theta and mid-frequency alpha and beta oscillations employ diverse physiological mechanisms determined by different ionic currents (Wang, 2010) and have distinct functional roles (Engel et al., 2001).
evidence: Supported by citation to Engel et al., 2001
